speechtext:

subtopic: HOSPITAL FACILITIES
speechtext:
1.	In mental hospitals, tuberculosis sanatoria, hospitals for chronically ill, hospitals for acute diseases and convalescent hospitals there is a definite shortage of beds.
The shortage of beds in mental hospitals, sanatoria, and for chronic and convalescent cases has existed over a period of years, but as regards hospitals for acute diseases the shortage has become acute only since 1940.
2.	For hospitals for acute diseases, it is estimated that there is need of an additional 8,000 beds to meet present needs, as calculated on the percentage of bed occupancy in those hospitals which in 1945 was 73-0 per cent.
As there were only ten convalescent hospitals in Canada in 1945 with a bed capacity of 800, and 17 hospitals for the chronically ill with 3,280 beds, there is great need of an increase in the number of hospitals in these two classes in order to release the beds now occupied by these classes of patients in hospitals for acute diseases.
According to hospital authorities beds for convalescent patients should form ten per cent
of total beds in public hospitals. On this basis there should be an additional 5,000 beds for use of convalescent patients and 3,000 for the chronically ill.
In 1945 there were 13,614 beds in tuberculosis institutions, and as the minimum standard of beds is based on three beds per death, at least 5,000 more beds are needed to meet present needs throughout Panada.
The number of beds reported for mental hospitals in 1945 was 45,124, while the number of patients in residence on December 31, 1945, was 48,056 (exclusive of patients on parole and in boarding homes, whose number amounted to 4,190). It is estimated that a minimum of 6,000 beds is needed to reduce the present overcrowding in mental hospitals.

On the orders of the day:
May I ask the Prime Minister if he is in a position to give the house a full statement with respect to the situation in India?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That is a tall order.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
May I say to my hon. friend that I would hesitate very much even to pretend to be able to make a full statement with respect to the situation in India. I believe it is one of the most critical and delicate situations existing in any part of the world today. However I was asked yesterday by the press if I had any comment to make with respect to the statement of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom as to what was proposed between the British government and India. I did give the press a statement,
and I think perhaps I could not answer my hon. friend's question better than to give the house just what I said at that time. I said this:
The peoples of India may be assured of the sympathetic understanding and good will of the government and people of Canada in their efforts to achieve self-government.
It is of the utmost importance to the future peace and prosperity of other countries, as well as of India, that this end should be peacefully achieved.
It may be taken for granted that once the Indian people as well as their leaders, have reached agreement on their future political status, they will find Canada generously predisposed towards self-government. The result may be to enlarge the number of states within the British commonwealth.

Mr. Speaker, I think the house should associate itself with that sentiment, which says in effect that Canada would be pleased to do everything she can to welcome into the family of the commonwealth the nation which we hope will now emerge in India.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask a question of the Prime Minister or the Secretary of State for External Affairs. An answer was given on Monday with respect to this same matter. I was told by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that we had a representative in India now, and that we would be informed if anything happened. Now we find that everything was consented to by the government of Canada; is that correct? Is the statement made by the minister at page 3708 of Hansard a correct statement?-because at that time the minister indicated the government had no knowledge of the matter at all. Surely the government must appreciate that the House of Commons cannot know anything about it unless it is informed.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have no doubt my right hon. friend the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. St. Laurent) may wish to say a word about this. If I understood my friend the hon. member for Broadview correctly he said there had been a statement to the effect that everything that had taken place in respect of developments in India had been consented to by the government of Canada. He wishes to know, as I understood him, whether that is correct and, if so, why the house was not informed. May I reply by saying that our government was kept informed by the government of the United Kingdom with respect to certain negotiations between the government of the United Kingdom and representatives from India. After what has now been made public as the agree-
Inquiries oj the Ministry

ment reached between them, our government was asked if we wished to make any comment. It would not be correct to say that we had been consulted during the negotiations because we were not consulted, but we were asked if we wished to make any comment. I have no exception to take to that method of procedure, because I do not think any other method would have been possible in the circumstances.
The reply which I have just given to the house will indicate the attitude which our government took in replying to the government of the United Kingdom as to what Canada's position would likely be in the event of new dominions being formed in India as a result of the negotiations that have been taking place.
It is going to cause civil war there, because they will not be ready for dominion status for years.
May I point out to the Prime Minister that the Canadian Press dispatch says that the Canadian government did approve the changed status in India.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know what dispatch my hon. friend has seen or has in mind, but I noticed when I picked up the morning paper that there was a statement to the effect that some high official had said that the government of Canada had been consulted. Speaking to one of my colleagues I drew attention to the fact that the particular word "consulted" had been used. I stated that that was what had repeatedly been said in regard to previous negotiations affecting the relations between different parts of the empire, but that what was really meant was that we had been kept informed of developments and had been asked if there was any comment we wish to make. This, however, was not until after the announcement had been made of the results of earlier negotiations. That to my mind is something different from consultation. As a matter of fact I doubt if it would have been possible for the government of the United Kingdom in making the arrangements with its dependency India to have tried to carry on those negotiations by consultation with the dominions.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Perhaps the house will allow me to supplement the remarks I made in reply to the hon. member for Broadview. I think it is important that the house should understand exactly what is expected of dominion governments in matters of consultation with the government of the United Kingdom. I find that the Secretary

of State for External Affairs answered a question asked on February 10 by the hon. member for Broadview with reference to possible negotiations concerning the Suez canal and Egypt, and the reply brought in the attitude and the relations of governments of the commonwealth in dealing with matters of this kind.
Again on February 24 the hon. member for Broadview asked:
Can the government inform the house of the present situation in India and Palestine?
Other questions were asked. One of the answers made at that time by the Secretary of State for External Affairs was as follows:
The present situation in India was outlined in a statement made on February 20 by the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom. The present situation in Palestine was outlined in a statement made in the United Kingdom parliament on February 18.
Commonwealth governments keep each other informed on matters of foreign policy in accordance with the practice described by Mr. Attlee, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, in the House of Commons in London, on May 8, 1946, as follows:
Then follows the paragraph which I wish particularly to diraw to the attention of hon. members. It is the statement of Mr. Attlee, Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, made in the House of Commons in London on May 8, 1946. He said:
It is our practice and our duty as members of the British commonwealth to keep other members of the commonwealth fully and continuously informed qf all matters which we are called upon to decide, but which may affect commonwealth interests. The object is to give them an opportunity of expressing their views in confidence, if they so desire. These view's are taken fully into account, but the decision must be ours, and the other governments are not asked, and would not wish, to share the responsibility for it. Dominion governments follow the same practice.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs went on to say:
This practice has been followed with regard to United Kingdom policy in India and Palestine.
I understand that on Monday the same answer was given to the hon. member for Broadview by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to a similar question.

Inquiries of the Ministry
I did not send him notice of it. It arises out of a press dispatch which in my opinion casts considerable reflection upon his own good judgment. I should like him to comment upon this. The press dispatch bears the date line New Glasgow, Nova Scotia, June 3, and it appeared in today's Ottawa Journal. subtopic: PERMIT FOR PROCESSING AND PACKING-SHORTAGE OF TIN-TOPPER INDUSTRIES LIMITED

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PERMIT FOR PROCESSING AND PACKING-SHORTAGE OF TIN-TOPPER INDUSTRIES LIMITED
speechtext:
A wire was sent to Mr. Fox who is president of the Legion in New Glasgow. A certain concern in New Glasgow, Topper Industries Limited, had obtained a permit to can chicken. They acquired a considerable quantity of seven ounce tin cans for that purpose. As the house knows, tin is in short supply and tin cans are strictly under allocation by the proper agency of the wartime prices and trade board. For one reason or another it was found that it was not commercially feasible to can and sell chicken, and an application was made to the board to use these cans for the purpose of putting up pork and beans. Permits for the canning of pork and beans have been strictly controlled for a number of years because of the shortage of tins and because of the large quantities of dried beans which we have to export to the United Kingdom. Manufacturers who were canning this particular product in 1941 have been held down to 60 per cent of their previous production and so far as I know no new canners have been allowed to go into this particular business. Everybody would like to go into the canning of pork and beans because there is a ready market and they can be easily sold, but there are not sufficient tins to enable that to be done. As I say, there has been considerable control over people putting up this particular product
and the wartime prices and trade board has had to refuse constantly applications of this kind.
There was no discrimination in this case.
I gave the matter careful personal consideration because I would have liked to have been able to ask to have this permission granted. However, I found that it could not be done after similar permission had been asked elsewhere and been refused. I have written to the gentleman in New Glasgow explaining the circumstances fully. That is the story. There has been no discrimination against this particular industry. I would have liked to see them get permission to do it, but it just could not be done. Incidentally, a seven ounce tin is not suitable for the canning of pork and beans.

subtopic: PERMIT FOR PROCESSING AND PACKING-SHORTAGE OF TIN-TOPPER INDUSTRIES LIMITED
speechtext: I should like to ask a supplementary question. Is the minister aware of the fact that the press statement states that this company has 400,000 tins on hand as well as the necessaiy beans and molasses? They claim that permission was refused because they were not doing business in 1941. They claim also that their chicken canning business went out of operation because they were refused an export permit.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PERMIT FOR PROCESSING AND PACKING-SHORTAGE OF TIN-TOPPER INDUSTRIES LIMITED
speechtext: I have given an explanation. I went into the situation very carefully. I am fully aware of the circumstances, but the same claim could be made by dozens, or probably a hundred other canners throughout Canada. That is the situation. We cannot issue permits for the further canning of pork and beans for the reason I have given.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
The minister yesterday made a short statement. If he will remember, when the resolution was up for consideration, he promised to make a statement about several different phases of this problem. For example, at page 2683 of Hansard he was asked:
Will the minister give us in some detail what his plan is for improving the penitentiary system ?
His answer was:
I think it would be more appropriate to do that at a later stage.
Again, at page 2686. he was asked about classification, segregation and after care, and in particular about the Borstal system. He said:
At a later stage I shall be prepared to discuss the Borstal system, and how far it is possible for the dominion government to do anything in the application of that system here in Canada. The whole problem is complicated by the division of responsibility between the federal and provincial governments, but probably it will not be impossible to apply certain features of the Borstal system, even in connection with some federal institutions.
At page 2687 he was asked how far the commissioner would be going in carrying out the recommendations that he had made in his report, and the minister replied that he would have to make a statement on that at a later day. There were also questions about calling a conference of the dominion and the provinces, and about giving aid to the prisoners' aid societies, and the minister said in respect to both these matters that he would make a statement later. Could he deal with these different, aspects of the problem today?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
What I had in mind was doing it on the penitentiary estimates rather than on this bill. This is a simple bill, as I have said. The principle of this bill can be summed up in just a sentence or two. I would prefer to discuss most of those matters fur-

Penitentiary Act
ther with the commissioner after he has been appointed commissioner of penitentiaries. Thus far that is not his position. He has prepared a report which was placed on the table of the house, and in that report it is recommended that in due course the construction of an additional penal institution in the province of Quebec be proceeded with, where the principles of the Borstal system in so far as possible would be applied. The division of constitutional responsibility as I understand it is something like this. Under section 92 of the British North America Act gaols and reformatories in and for the province are under the jurisdiction of the province, and by section 91 penitentiaries are under the jurisdiction of the dominion. If the dominion were to construct and administer an institution which is not a penitentiary it would have to be one which would not come within the words "in and for a province." It would have to be an institution which extended to more than one province. Within these limitations it is thought that it would be possible to undertake the administration and control of reformatory institutions. I take it that these Borstal institutions could be described as reformatories; I do not think that they can properly be described as penitentiaries. Of course the situation is complicated by the fact that simply because the dominion may have the power to administer reformatories, provided the scope of their operation is extended to more than one province, it does not mean that they should do so if they are to duplicate the work of provincial institutions directed to a similar object. Therefore I am sure it would be necessary to work more closely in cooperation with the provinces.
The only institution as to which there is any degree of definiteness about the plans is the one mentioned for French-speaking convicts. I gather from what my hon. friend says that the province of Quebec is making plans for a reformatory institution. If there is a duplication there that is something which would have to be considered between the dominion and the provincial authorities so that we would not be covering the same ground.
With regard to the prisoners' aid societies, General Gibson came to the conclusion, after making a study of plans for after care, that the simple and probably the most practical plan for providing for that care was by financial assistance to prisoners' aid societies. From conversations with him my impression is that they are not far enough advanced; that is, they are not quite in a position to establish that their activities would be effective, that their activities are the kind of activities that we would want to assist them in financially.
When I say that the financial plans are indefinite I mean that the matter of finances, as I said before, has to be authorized by the governor in council and by the treasury board; but so far as I am concerned I would be disposed to accept and act on, as a very practical measure of advance, of progress, the report which I secured from General Gibson and which was placed before the house some time ago. Without reflecting upon the Archam-bault report, I think this report is a more practical one than the scheme for an over-all inclusive centralization and an elaborate organization. The Gibson report is the report that I think we should proceed on for the time being, and I would recommend that we do so.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I notice that by section 1 of this bill there is to be added to section 2 of the Penitentiary Act the words "prison reformatories." I suppose that is because the department have in mind setting up the Borstal system.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I think that is based upon the theory that we can deal only with penitentiaries. For the reasons that I have stated it may not be strictly true. It may be that we have jurisdiction also over penal institutions which are not penitentiaries, provided that they are not penal institutions in and for a province. I think this section is based upon the safer ground that we can administer only penitentiaries. This gives the governor in council power to designate certain prisons, prison reformatories and public institutions as penitentiaries.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: The minister thinks it would be impossible to establish the Borstal system without some arrangement having been made between the dominion and the provinces?

I want to make one comment on the point raised by the hon. member for Vancouver South. Like him, I am disappointed that the
Penitentiary Act

minister has decided that more extensive remarks by him should be made when the estimates come up, and I venture to hope that we shall not find that it is hurried or crowded, because I do feel that we wrant what I might call a full dress speech from the minister on this subject. I for one will be tremendously disappointed if the federal authorities cannot introduce in their penitentiaries some programme for the reclamation of what I called yesterday first offenders who are sent to the penitentiary-I am not referring now to persons committed to gaols in the provinces. Did I understand the minister to say that such a programme cannot be introduced into the penitentiaries? It might necessitate one penitentiary being selected for that type of criminal. A conference of the provinces is not necessary.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

He does not need to be twenty-one, nineteen or eighteen to commit a crime serious enough to be sentenced to a penitentiary for over two years; it may be for three or four years, depending on the offence. They are there for the first time, but their crime *was sufficiently serious to necessitate their being sent to the penitentiary. I think that is what is proposed to be done by the Gibson report. We propose to start in that way. But first offenders, if they are not sentenced to the penitentiary, are under provincial jurisdiction. In the province of Quebec there are reformatory

institutions for those young offenders. As far as we are concerned here, we contemplate doing something for these young offenders, putting them in some other institution and beginning with the application of the Borstal system.

Apart from that, I was going to ask two or three questions under (f). I presume all the instructors mentioned under (f), which include bakers, blacksmiths and so forth, are of the type we have now in our penitentiaries. Have we not all those now in our penitentiaries?

speechtext:
In connection with such employees may I ask the following questions? I am not particular whether I get an answer now or not. I will just read them as they are written out here:
1.	What, if any, are the civil service regulations respecting applicants for appointment to the civil service who have criminal records?

After all, somebody has to give jobs to those who are released from prison. I myself have spent many hours trying to find jobs for men who have been let out of different types of penal institutions. If they cannot get a job and an opportunity to earn their living, they will go back to what they were into before, or
worse. I have obtained many positions for men of that type, and the vast majority of them have made good.
I have asked four questions, but they do not need to be answered now.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I am not in a position to answer those questions. I do not know what the rules of the civil service commission are.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I have no doubt the Department of Justice is sincere in trying to improve our penal system. The whole question is whether the legislation now before us is going to effect any important improvement. I think the question asked by the hon. member for Kindersley requires a little more attention than the minister gave to it. It is not a question of the qualifications of General Gibson. I doubt whether any individual could possess all the qualifications required for the performance of the duties he will have to perform. No doubt he is a competent executive. No doubt he is an honest and able man. But he is not likely to be a psychiatrist, and he is not likely to be a philosopher. He is not likely to know a great deal about the social background from which crime emerges, and would not be in a position to make decisions either with respect to general policy or with respect to individuals who may come under his attention. I think it is important that there should be a commission rather than an individual, so that we may have represented on that commission all these important sciences and the whole question may be considered in its fullest scope. I think that is, in the main, what this legislation lacks. Has the minister given his last word with regard to enlarging that commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: Yes. That matter has been fully considered, both by myself and by the government, and we decided that this was the most efficient way in which to set the commission up.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I understood the minister to contend that if a man is convicted and sentenced to less than two years, even under the criminal code, he must be sent to the provincial prison.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER

Surely we could establish our own prisons to which persons could be committed who had been found guilty of violations of the criminal code or some other federal law. I know we do nc t. wish to duplicate these prisons, but as far as the constitu-

tional question is concerned, surely we could establish our own prisons for these people who are convicted under federal law. Is that not the true situation?

Section agreed to.
On section 2-Commissioner.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
As I understand it this section amends the Penitentiary Act, 1939, to provide for the appointment of a commissioner of penitentiaries and two deputy commissioners, who are to perform such duties as are assigned to them by the commissioner. In other words the commissioner is to be in complete charge of our penal institutions and the deputies, if I read the act correctly, are to be responsible to the commissioner and not to parliament. This change in the act of 1939 fails to follow the recommendations of the Arehambault royal commission, which suggested that a commission be set up in Canada similar to that which operates in Great Britain. There the prison commission is composed of a chairman and two commissioners, one of whom is an administrator while the other is a medical expert. Each member in turn is responsible to the British parliament for the work of his department, and is not responsible to the chairman of the commission. This section of our act leaves the responsibility of operating our penal system in the hands of one man. It is indeed a very heavy responsibility. At page 342 of the report of the royal commission to investigate the penal system of Canada I note the following comment:
In our present system the problem of penal administration is too large in scope and too serious in results to be left in the hands of one man.
The report made by that commission is considered by penologists to be an excellent piece of work. I am no authority on the subject, but I have read what others have said. These men were experts in their own fields. They must have been qualified or the government would not have appointed them in the first place. ' Their report was based on experience and information obtained by visiting penal institutions not only in Canada but

other countries as well. This amendment is based on the report of one man; that is, the present commissioner of penitentiaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: No, he did not recommend that the board be reduced to one man.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: That may be so, Mr. Chairman, but the fact remains that the Archam-bault commission did recommend that the penitentiary commission be set up on the lines of the commission in Great Britain. In view of that fact I feel that an attempt is being made here, as it has been made throughout this whole bill, to sidetrack the recommendations of the Arehambault commission; and I feel that any amendment to the Penitentiary Act should be in keeping with the recommendations of that commission, because I believe these men made a thorough study of the situation and spent a good deal of time on that study. I cannot conceive of one man devoting such a short time to the study of penal institutions and submitting to the minister a report which would be accepted so readily, unless there is some reason for it; and I suggest the reason is that the recommendations of the Arehambault royal commission did not meet with the approval of the government. Therefore I must register my protest against this contemplated change, and I shall certainly vote against it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
I should like to direct attention to subsection 4, which provides that the commissioner and the deputy commissioners shall be paid such salaries as are approved by the governor in council. I am not so much interested in the salaries of the heads of the branch, and then working down; I would like to start at the bottom and work up. I have in mind the junior officials of the penitentiary branch. I hold in my hand a copy of the Gibson report, in which at page 9 I find this statement:
As a result of increases granted by the government in 1945 and the recent incorporation of the cost of living bonus in the permanent salaries of the lower brackets, the pay of prison guards now has a range of $1,704-$2,004 per annum.
Then listen to this:
There has not, however, been a proportionate increase in the middle and higher ranges of salaries of penitentiary employees, and in your commissioner's opinion a revision of salary rates is necessary to extend to these groups a similar proportionate increase and to provide a rate of remuneration that will attract to and retain in the service the necessary qualified senior officers, professional personnel and trade instructors required for the efficient administration of the penitentiaries and the carrying out of the reforms contemplated by the royal commission's report. This recommendation has already been submitted for consideration in con-

Judges Act
nection with the survey of salaries in the government service now' being carried out by officials of the treasury board.
Can the right hon. gentleman inform the committee whether those recommendations have been put into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: I think they have, but I am not sure. The salary scale now is as follows. An officer entering the penitentiary service as a guard now receives an initial salary of $1,740 per annum, rising by annual increases to $2,040, as compared with a range of $1,200 to $1,500 prior to 1945. Provision has been made for a higher grade of guard, representing twenty per cent of the total, who may receive salaries up to $2,280 per annum. A corresponding increase for all grades of the service has been authorized. For example, keepers now range from $2,220 to $2,580; chief keepers from $2,700 to $3,300; instructors from $2,100 to $2,580; chief trade instructors from $2,700 to $3,300; deputy wardens from $3,600 to $4,500, and wardens from $4,800 to $6,000. These new rates came into effect from January 1, 1947.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: What date was that put into effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR APPOINTMENT OF COMMISSIONER
speechtext: They came into effect as from January 1, 1947, and they were put into effect by order in council P.C. 66/1050 of March 22, 1947.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

speechtext:
Right Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Justice) moved that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a measure to amend the Judges Act, 1946, to change the title of the Superior Court judge in and for the province of Quebec, who is appointed to perform the duties of the Chief Justice in the district as constituted for the Court of King's Bench sitting in appeal within which the chief justice does not reside. Montreal or Quebec, as the case may be, to "The Associate Chief Justice"; and to provide a salary for an additional judge of the Supreme Court of British Columbia.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Golding in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some members have asked for an explanation. The first part of the resolution is rendered necessary by a recent change in the statutes of Quebec which provides for the appointment of an associate chief justice in that province. Until that amendment was passed by the Quebec legislature in 1946 there was an acting chief justice

Judges Act

in that province. Now the acting chief justice is to be known as the associate chief justice.
There are two districts, the Quebec district and the Montreal district. If the chief justice resides in one district, the acting chief justice is appointed to reside in the other district. Under this provision the acting chief justice is to be called the associate chief justice. There is no difference in the pay he is to receive under this legislation, beyond that which he received before. This measure simply makes our legislation conform with that in Quebec.
The second part of the resolution is to provide the salary for an additional supreme court judge in British Columbia. Strong representations have been made that another judge is required in that province. While these representations are made often, and are not confined to British Columbia, and while I hope every minister of justice will be hard to convince when he receives these representations, I have been convinced that an additional judge is badly needed in British Columbia.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

Rightly or wrongly,
the general public are of the opinion that at present judges are able to attend to their duties without any great strain upon their health. speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
It is difficult to settle the
question whether there is real need for another judge, but in the case of British Columbia I have had letter after letter from the chief justice of the trial division and I have a considerable volume of correspondence with the attorney general. There is no objective test that you can apply to determine whether there is a need. The proportion of judges to the population or the proportion of judges to the members of the bar and so on is not a correct test to apply. A certain proportion may be proper for one province and not proper for another. There is really nothing you can do except to inquire and find out whether they really need one. In this case we have an abundance of material which I can show to my hon. friend if he would like to see it. It consists of long lists of cases, information as to when they will be reached and what will have to be done if they are to keep within a mile of transacting the necessary business. In view of the immigration
from Saskatchewan and other provinces to British Columbia I have no doubt that we do need one or two more trial judges to look after the extra business. One way of arriving

at the need would be to give us some idea of the number of trials which each judge *conducts each term, how long each trial lasted, and so on. I wonder where the new judge will reside. Will it be in Cariboo, for example? We ought to have a new judge up there, because it is a long way from Victoria or Vancouver and there is a tremendous country to cover.

He will probably reside in Vancouver or Victoria and then go out on circuit. Speaking for my own province, I know that is the system. No matter from what part of the province the judge may be appointed, he resides in Halifax and then goes out through the province.
Mr. CRUICIvSHANK: Will the minister consider appointing the hon. member for Vancouver South?-because that would be a good way to get rid of him.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: The minister has not been very long in the department but I should like to call his attention to a great injustice that exists in Ontario as compared with our very fine sister province with regard to judges' titles, style of work done, volume of work done and so on. I ask the minister to consider my observations and see what can be done. Judge Parker was a very fine lawyer and he has given excellent satisfaction. subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: There are anomalies there that should be looked into and corrected.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

Previous to the legislation the provision was for the appointment of a judge to perform the duties of the chief justice, and I think he was called the acting chief justice. subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: It is merely to provide for the payment of salary to the judge who is described in the amendment,

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: That is true.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
out taking into consideration any of the incidental emoluments of office, and in those days there was no income tax. I merely point that out to show that, in the land where justice is dispensed in a way that all peoples admire, judges have been well paid and for that reason I was happy some months ago to support legislation to increase the salaries of the judges.
Turning to British Columbia we must be guided. I suppose, by the information which the minister has as to the necessity of appointing an additional judge for that province. I wish, however, that the minister could assure the committee that this judge and the judges in the other provinces are required for work that is strictly judicial. In my opinion the tendency of the last few years has been to use judges for the solution of problems which are not, in their nature, judicial but highly political, and in my view that has tended to lessen the respect and confidence of the people at large in the judiciary. That is a great misfortune, and if I have found it necessary to express these views more than once in the house it is because of my intimate knowledge of the situation and because of my conviction of the degrading tendency that this practice has upon the good repute of the individual judge and of the bench of which he forms part. My remarks have as their sole object to preclude any further use of judges as part of committees or -commissions dealing with other than legal problems, because the rule of law depends largely for its efficacy upon the respect and confidence which the people repose in the 'bench.
To be altogether objective. I must refer to -what is called the spy case. Two judges of our highest court, the Supreme Court of Canada, were asked to act as commissioners. Their appointment denatured them as judges. They ceased to exercise judicial functions. They were put at tasks which were not judicial. I think the minister is familiar with what is known as the O'Connor case. O'Connor when acting as a commissioner did something which was reprehensible and I believe that the highest tribunal, the privy council, found that in that instance he was acting as a persona designate. Certain immunities went with the .task, but it goes to show that there is a distinction between the role of the judge and rthe role of the man who acts, as these two -gentlemen did; when they presided oyer the spy investigation. We have heard these men criticized; and again I say that I do not wish to be critical of the government in that particular instance. We were just emerging from a war; we were not accustomed to spies in [DOT].this country. More is known of them in
JMr. Hackett.]
older and more developed countries. The government appointed these two men to that task. I do not blame them, They accepted what they undoubtedly conceived to be a call to duty; nevertheless the fact is that two judges of our highest court have been criticized bitterly. They have not been criticized by irresponsible people; they have been criticized by the press of the country; they have been criticized from the pulpits of the country and-I do not know whether the minister is aware of it-they have been criticized from the bench of the country, from the appeal benches of at least two provinces.
It is extremely unfortunate that a condition should be created in which men who hold such important positions, whose impartiality and integrity must at all times be beyond reproach, should be so criticized. It is because of the practice of setting them tasks which are not judicial that this criticism has come about, and the result has been, and must necessarily be. a loss of dignity, loss of confidence, loss of respect by the individuals themselves as well as by the bench of which they form a part.
Let us suppose that one of the men or women was found-I do not know that I should say guilty, but as a result of the finding of these two judges, was prosecuted and was later found guilty-and the case went, as many of them have, to an appellate tribunal, and there was a further appeal to the supreme court. There is an appeal to the supreme court, but it is a limited one. I ask, hon. gentlemen, what would be the feeling of a person so accused finding himself before the supreme court? I am certain that neither of these honourable judges would sit upon the case. Nevertheless their brethren, those who labour with them and who have respect for their feelings, for their integrity and for their wisdom, would be called upon to determine a case on which two of their brother judges had already pronounced themselves. To admit this possibility establishes that the practice is indefensible.
A few days ago when the hon. member for Winnipeg North was making some comment, which I thought was most unfortunate, on the conduct of these gentlemen I had something to say on this topic. An attempt was made to stop the hon. gentleman because he was exceeding his privileges as a member of parliament. I besought the hon. gentleman to desist from further criticism, but I was forced to argue that he had the right to say what he was saying, and I doubt whether any Speaker could, after consideration, hold otherwise. Nevertheless a few days afterwards another gifted and able member of the supreme court was appointed to a committee

Judges Act
whose task is the hearing and the determination of one of the most highly political questions that has tortured this country in the last century. I yield to no one in my respect of Mr. Justice Rand, but I consider it a tragedy that he should be lifted out of his judicial office and asked to participate in an investigation and settlement of a political question. Whatever the decision, he cannot return to his judicial function without some people believing, and unfortunately some people saying that he has been influenced by this or that motive, that he has sided with this or that political faction. It is not fitting such sentiment or words should be provoked by a judge.
In Canada we have not many institutions that have not been shaken by the events of the last few years. Our civilization, like all civilizations, rests on great institutions: the Christian home, the school, the church and the law, and they have all been very much manhandled in the last few years. The result is that civilization has crumbled in many parts of Europe and in many parts of the world. Even if we did nothing more than expose one of these fundamental institutions to weakness by the appointment of members of the judiciary to duties which are beyond their scopes, it seems to me that the hazard is too great to be taken by a responsible government. It is clear that the hon. gentlemen who have appointed judges to these tasks do not share my view. Can it be that their present occupations are so manifold, that they are so remote from the common touch that they do not appreciate to what extent this great institution of the law is jeopardized and imperilled by the action which has become the habit in the last few years?
I have said previously that other governments have appointed judges to perform tasks of this kind. I thought it reprehensible then. The courts did not benefit by it, and a number of judges still suffer as a result of services which they rendered off the bench.
I am going to appeal again to the Minister of Justice, with whom I cannot always agree hut for whom I have immeasurable respect, to consider most carefully the result of discrediting the judiciary. We cannot afford to do it at this time. The rule of law has never been so seriously challenged as it is today. If we cannot, here in Canada, maintain the fullest confidence in our judiciary, we are heading for unnecessary evils. We have all kinds of difficulties. I know the government has to meet as many complicated and seemingly insoluble problems as any government that has ever occupied the treasury benches.
While it is the function of the opposition to criticize and endeavour to improve administration, this is a matter which really transcends politics. I ask the government to desist from this practice. We have labour troubles, financial difficulties, and problems of great variety. I cannot help feeling that the appointment of judges to solve all these problems does not rest solely on the fact that all the able men in Canada are on the bench. I cannot believe that. But I do believe that the great reputation of the judiciary-the confidence the public has in its members-has prompted the government at times to shield itself from criticism by naming a judge to such a commission.
Again I say to the Minister of Justice that I have not heard many judges approve this practice; I have not heard many lawyers approve it and I have not heard many people who understood it thoroughly approve it. If another judge in British Columbia be required for the purpose of administering justice, let him be appointed; but. let us keep him within the ambit of his judicial function, and let us terminate once and for all the submission to members of the judiciary of questions which are not legal and which do not come within the proper performance of their duties.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I was going to say a word with regard to the appointment of the additional judge in British Columbia, but I think the hon. member for Cariboo has said pretty much what I would have said, namely, that the only criterion which can apply as to whether there are sufficient judges is the amount of court work that is behind schedule, as we might say. If cases are being held for a long time without coming to trial, or if judges are overworked in the matter of trials, then, of course, a case could be made out for the appointment of an additional judge. However, the decision to appoint one has been made by the present Minister of Justice, and I do not know of anyone less likely to give way to pressure than the right hon. gentleman. I have come to that conclusion from watching him resist pressure in this house over a long period of time. Therefore I have no misgivings on that point.
I know it is presumptuous on my part to say anything in regard to the matter referred to by the hon. member for Stanstead, but I think it would be a retrograde step for the
Judges Act

government to take if it were to decide that members of the judiciary should not function as commissioners in certain instances.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Hear, hear. They have done it in Britain for hundreds of years.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: Whether a mistake was made in appointing judges in the espionage investigations is open to question, and I am not expressing any opinion in regard' to it. It is a case of a kind which I think has never before arisen in this country. From my association with the labour movement over a long period of time, I believe that organized labour has, in general, more confidence in a judge as chairman of a board than it would have in any person from almost any other walk of life. Generally speaking, I think the judges have, in the discharge of these special duties, given satisfaction and have done so without affecting their position as judges. I am afraid that the point of view expressed by the hon. member for Stanstead-who is, I may tell him, a man for whom I have the greatest respect-is old-fashioned. I do not think it is wise today to keep the judiciary separate from what we might call the hurly-burly of everyday life because they are not just dispensing law; they are dispensing justice. It may be justice according to the law, but I think it should be justice as far as they can go, even if they went beyond the law. However I imagine that is not good law.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext: It is common sense.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
If you keep the judges apart from the ordinary, everyday interests and trials of the people, how are they to acquire the understanding to make just decisions in the cases which come before them? Judges I believe, follow precedents in cases which have gone before, no matter whether those decisions were right or wrong. I do not think that is good enough. I think it would be a great mistake if this government took any action which would prevent judges from acting on commissions where their position carries weight. I think that is so for the very reasons advanced by the hon. member for Stanstead. When they are appointed to the bench judges are given a reasonable standard of living; they

are given security; they are given a standing in the community, and it is a lifetime appointment. Consequently when a judge is made chairman of a commission, or a commissioner, he can act without any hope of reward from the outside or any fear of punishment from the inside. So I think we should consider carefully before we change that situation.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I wish to make a few comments on this resolution. First, I want to say I am pleased that provision is being made for the appointment of another judge in British Columbia. I remember that this matter came up when I was in the provincial house, and some three or four years ago the former attorney general told me of the great need for another judge in that province. I think anyone who has followed the work of the courts there is aware of the need for another judge in British Columbia; and in this case, as the hon. member for Vancouver East suggested, I think the Minister of Justice resisted pressure for a considerable time.
I was very much interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for Stanstead as to the use of members of the judiciary on arbitrations and so on. To some extent I agree with the spirit of his remarks; I can see the point in some of his arguments, but I do not believe you can make a fixed, general rule in these matters. Over a period of years I have had occasion to act on behalf of labour on several quite important arbitration boards in British Columbia, in connection with shipyards and so on, which dealt with difficult and, at times, trying situations. In that case I may say I went straight from the farm to represent labour, without any former experience in that regard. All hon. members know, when arbitration boards are appointed the representative of the employers and the representative of the employees are supposed to meet and agree on a chairman; otherwise I understand the chairman is appointed by the Minister of Labour. In the first place, of course it is necessary to have someone who has some knowledge of the rules of evidence, someone who can be of assistance to laymen in directing the work of the inquiry. I was quite surprised to find that in each case with which I was directly connected organized labour expressed great satisfaction over being able to secure a judge as chairman of the tribunal. I remember one board on which I served; I think the hon. member for Vancouver Centre will remember the shipyards case, with which it dealt. We agreed on one of the judges, who was appointed chairman. Those negotiations went on over a period of three months, under conditions which at times were difficult and trying. I was inter-

Judges Act
ested to note that at first many of the representatives of labour and members of unions were inclined to look upon the representative of the judiciary as someone apart, someone possibly not quite human. But as the arbitration went on I saw that they became impressed with his fairness, and their confidence in the impartial attitude of the judiciary was greatly increased.
So in my view, far from the appointment of judges to boards of arbitration and things of that kind lowering their position or lessening the respect felt by people generally for the judiciary, my experience has been that, during recent times by these rather unusual contacts with the judiciary, such appointments have brought about increased respect for members of the bench on the part of representatives of labour and others throughout this country. Many of the men engaged in these investigations were not Conservative, to say the least, in their politics, but they expressed to me their confidence in and appreciation of the work done by these gentlemen. So, while I am sure none of us would wish to see members of the judiciary used for these purposes too extensively, I am also sure that under certain conditions in this country it is necessary and to the advantage of the parties concerned and the community at large that the services of these gentlemen be made available. To that extent I believe it would heighten respect throughout this country for the members of the judiciary.

subtopic: ASSOCIATE CHIEF JUSTICE, PROVINCE OF QUEBEC- ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN BRITISH COLUMBIA
speechtext:
I wish to speak on the
amendment to the Judges Act, 1946, which provides for the appointment of an additional judge in British Columbia. Under the British North America Act, the provinces have responsibility for the organization of these courts. The year before last Ontario had two additional judges appointed. In my opinion the Judges Act should be revised and brought up to date. It was first passed a very long time ago and. with the exception of minor changes, has not been revised since about the time the Supreme Court Act was passed in 1875.
I want to point out that the work of the provincial courts has been greatly increased, largely as a result of legislation passed by this parliament. For example, there is the matter of divorce. Immediately that act was passed Ontario applied for two or three more high court judges, and their salaries have to be paid by the dominion government. Some of the judges have been sick; others have been away on commissions. When Saskatchewan applied for an additional judge we found that one of those already appointed
had been away on commissions practically all his time. Some change should be made in that regard.
Then all the judges appointed under this act are governed by the doctrine of stare decisis, which means by decisions of the privy council or court of last resort; but in one province they have not followed that law. There will always be a privy council, notwithstanding the bill introduced here the other day, because that legislation binds only the dominion. It does not bind the provinces, which can give the right to appeal direct to the king as a matter of grace. These privy council appeals are by statute or by grace, and the subject has always had the right to appeal to the throne as a matter of grace. That, of course, is not to the judicial committee of the privy council, which is delegated by the sovereign to hear such appeals.
Great care should be exercised in connection with these matters. In the United States they are having the same trouble. In that country, once you are sworn in as a lawyer you are immediately called "judge." You may not be a judge today, but probably you will be one tomorrow, so down there everyone who is a lawyer is called a judge. I would like the minister, in considering judicial appointments, not to make them from a purely political point of view. Sir John A. Macdonald often appointed people from the other side, and he made some very good appointments. It is difficult to get some of the judges who are appointed to carry on the work. We have twelve high court judges on circuit in Ontario, some of whom have not been out on circuit as much as others or are sick or at times on commissions. speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the bill based on this resolution is to provide for the refunding of Canadian National Railway securities in the years 1947 to 1954. The last refunding act was passed in 1944 for the same amount, namely $200,000,000. Canadian National Railway bonds that mature and are callable up to the end of 1954 total $221,304.943.61. The procedure outlined in the bill for meeting these maturities is either by refunding issues or by way of loan from the government. Since the outbreak of the war, only one railway issue, that of January 2. 1947, has been sold to the public. Other maturing issues have been met by loans from the government. The January 2, 1947, issue consisted of $50,000,000 twenty-year bonds at 2? per cent and was sold at 100-68, to yield 2-7 per cent. The resolution provides for the renewal of these loans.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR REFUNDING OF FINANCIAL OBLIGATIONS
speechtext:
Of course it is desirable that this refunding should be done. The only question I wish to raise is as to giving authority for refunding operations for the next five, six or seven years. You may argue: Why not do it because it is only giving authority which will not be abused? On the other hand. I myself cannot 83166-2424
see why we should now give authority extending over several years. I notice that in the railway committee the question was asked whether the reason why this authority should be given was that it was proposed to take advantage of the present low interest rates and go out and get the money, but the official of the company said no. I quote from page 149 of the report of proceedings, where he said:
We shall only issue new securities as of the date the old securities maturing are called. We will not secure funds in advance of need.
I am not making any comment as to whether or not it is wise; whether they would be well advised to go out and get $200 million now. There are complications in the way of it and I think reasons given against it may be quite valid. I do not criticize that. The point I wish to make is this. It seems to me a free and easy way of dealing with this matter, to give authority now which is to extend over five or six or seven years. If I am asked what difficulties can arise I confess quite frankly that I find it difficult to answer that. There may be changes in rates of interest. There may be reasons why this refunding later on may not appear as desirable as it is now. The minister may well say that if that occasion should arise, do I not think the railway officials are as competent as anyone to deal with it? My answer would be that they are very competent indeed. Nevertheless I can see no reason for it at the moment. By looking at page 149 of the report, I observe that there are only some $45 million callable as early as 1948. There are two amounts of $25 million and $20 million. Then there is a large issue which is callable in 1949 and another in 1950.
Without labouring the point further. I raise the question, first of all, whether it is necessary to do it. It seems simple to come along next year and bring in another resolution to give another authority. That is very simple indeed. We have to do that, of course, in connection with the amounts which are to be raised for extensions and improvements. That is done as a matter of course each year. I suggest to the committee that this is an unnecessary free and easy way of giving wide-open authorities to authorize $200 million now, when actually up to the end of 1948, if my reading is correct, only $45 million is necessary.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA

speechtext:
Right Hon. L. S. ST. LAURENT (Secretary of State for External Affairs) moved the

second reading of Bill No. 253, to make provision with respect to forces of the United States of America when visiting Canada and with respect to the exercise of discipline and to the internal administration of such forces.
He said: The purpose of this legislation is to make provision for the discipline of United States forces when visiting Canada. Hon. members know that there was passed by this parliament in 1933 an act, chapter 21 of the statutes of that year, making provision for the discipline of forces of commonwealth countries visiting Canada. At the outbreak of war, by an order in council under the War Measures Act this was extended to United States forces, and by -a subsequent order in council under the War Measures Act much broader provisions were made for the service courts of the United States, even to the exclusion of the jurisdiction of our Canadian courts.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
May I ask the minister a question? Did that order in council extend the powers under the Visiting Forces from Commonwealth Countries Act or under what was called foreign forces order?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: The first extended the provisions of the visiting forces of the commonwealth to -foreign forces present in Canada.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
By a foreign forces order?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: By a foreign forces order. Then there was a subsequent order in council giving more extensive jurisdiction to the service courts of United States forces than was provided by the foreign forces order; but both these orders lapsed or were repealed in compliance with the undertaking that had been, given in the house, on April 1 last, -because they were not included in the schedule to the so-called omnibus bill. Since that time, there has been no authority under which commanders of forces of the United States visiting Canada, on invitation or with the consent of the Canadian government, could exercise disciplinary powers, and the bill is to give the commanders of these forces powers similar to those which are provided in the act of 1933 with respect to the commonwealth forces, and particularly not to exclude the jurisdiction of the Canadian courts.
The purpose of this bill is to give the commanders of such visiting forces rights to exercise such jurisdiction as our own service courts can exercise in our own domestic armed units. But on the same principle, our own service courts do not oust the ordinary jurisdiction of the ordinary courts of the land. This provides that the jurisdiction given to the service courts of the United States will not oust

Visiting Forces
the jurisdiction of the ordinary courts of the land. The service courts of the United States will have exclusive jurisdiction in connection with such breaches of discipline as would not be offences under Canadian law. But with respect to anything which, though a breach of their military orders, would also be a breach of Canadian law, they get no exclusive jurisdiction. The statute also provides that such jurisdiction as they may exercise will be only over members of their forces, and that their decision as to who is a member of their forces will not be conclusive. If they attempt to exercise any of those powers in Canada with respect to an individual, and he claims not to be a member of their forces, the question as to whether he is a member of their forces will have to be determined by our own courts.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
That was, essentially, the
arrangement which existed during the war, was it not?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: No. During the war we went farther than that. Under United States law, their service courts have exclusive jurisdiction over their own personnel in their own country, to the exclusion of their own ordinary courts of justice; and they tell us that under their law our service courts would have, in their country, over personnel of Canadian forces visiting their country, jurisdiction that would be exclusive of their courts. But we told them that was not the principle which applied in British countries. We told them that in British countries the personnel of the army, like all other citizens, were amenable to the courts of justice of the country and that, although we did, because of the special conditions which existed during the war, make them that concession, it was only for the duration of the war. They have made representations to us, but we have told them that we could not give their service courts exclusive powers which our service courts did not have over the personnel of our own Canadian forces, and that they would have to be satisfied with exercising the jurisdiction they have by virtue of their law, but not to a greater extent than our laws recognized the jurisdiction of our own service courts. Moreover, we made it a provision that this jurisdiction would, of course, apply only to members of their forces, and that the question as to whether or not, in a concrete case, a person was amenable to their jurisdiction would have to be one which was triable by our ordinary courts of justice.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
Would the minister permit a question?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: Yes.

subtopic: UNITED STATES-DISCIPLINE AND INTERNAL ADMINISTRATION WHEN IN CANADA
speechtext:
What is the statutory or other source of power for the government to admit to Canada the armed forces of other nations outside the commonwealth?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: I do not think it makes any difference whether they be within or outside the commonwealth. We made with the United States government the informal arrangement which the Prime Minister described in this house on February 12. 1947, in a statement on defence cooperation. In that statement the Prime Minister outlined the programme of post-war cooperation between the armed forces of the United States and Canada resulting from discussions which had taken place in the permanent joint board on defence. This programme calls for the interchange of selected individuals so as to increase . the familiarity of each country's defence establishment with that of the other country. It also calls for general cooperation and exchange of observers in connection with exercises and with the development and tests of material of common interest. It encourages common designs and standards in arms, equipment, organization, methods of training and new developments. It provides for such extension of reciprocal military, naval and air facilities in each country as may be agreed upon in specific instances. It also provides, of course, that everything which is done by one country in the territory of the other is subject to the full control of the other country, recognizing the full sovereignty of the other country.
As an illustration of what is taking place, there is a small detachment of United States observers who have been stationed at Churchill taking part in the tests of material under the climatic conditions which exist there, but they are all under the supreme command of the Canadian commander of the post. He does not, however, attempt to exercise authority over the individuals. He does that through the normal chain of authority. speechtext:
Is there not this difference: These are armed forces of another nation?
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If the hon. member will just let me continue my exposition, there will be opportunity later for criticism. It is difficult when the house is not in committee to deal with these questions as they arise.
There is no statutory authority for the admission into Canada of the diplomatic representatives of other states. These are matters which are governed by the comity of nations; and I think it is the same with respect to the penetration within our country of the armed forces of another friendly state. If we resented it, it would be an unfriendly act for them to come. If we do not object to it, there is no need of statutory authority to enable its being done.
But of course they have no status as military units in this country, unless that is provided for by statute. And it is for that reason precisely that this bill is submitted to parliament. It is submitted to parliament, so that they can, when in fact here as a unit, be treated by those who are commanding them in the manner provided by military law, without that being an assault on, or with its being an interference with the individual liberty of the persons concerned.

Visiting Forces
Without something of this kind, no attempt, for instance, to arrest one of their members would be anything but a common assault. No attempt to restrain the movement of one of their members could be upheld in the face of a writ of habeas corpus. They would be merely a certain number of individuals, each recognized as individuals, and no one of them having any right to interfere with any movement of any other one of them. It is to take care of what is required for the proper discipline of a group coming under the command of officers that it is necessary to have some provision of this kind.
The provision to be made is that when United States forces are present in Canada the service courts and service authorities of those forces may exercise within Canada, in relation to members of those forces, all such powers as are conferred upon them by the laws of their own country; but not to the exclusion of the exercise by the ordinary authorities in this country of our own laws, and not to the exclusion of the rights of any person over whom they attempt to exercise that authority to apply to our own courts to determine whether or not he is a member of their forces.
This bill is to be concerned only with United States forces present in Canada with the consent, of the Canadian government. United States forces present in Canada without, the consent of the Canadian government would be committing an unfriendly act. This bill will have no application to civilians, or to any others than members of an organized unit of the United States present in our country with the consent of the Canadian authorities.
That is the same situation which had to be dealt with, or which it was felt should be dealt with by the Visiting Forces (British Common-weath) Act of 1933. Prior to that act, any group of persons from another part of the commonwealth could come here; there was nothing to prevent their coming here. But there was no right of anyone conducting such a party to exercise any authority in this country over the members of the party he was conducting. It was for that reason that the Visiting Forces (British Commonwealth) Act of 1933 was enacted, so that when groups came here-

Mr. Speaker, as the right, hon. minister has stated, this bill makes provision for those troops of the United States forces which are visiting Canada, so that their code of discipline may be applied through such military courts and through such other means as are expedient. It also enables the exercise of the internal administration of those forces.
In section 2, the expression "United States force" is clearly defined as one which is here in Canada, with the consent of the government of Canada, and is lawfully present in Canada or on board any of His Majesty's Canadian ships or aircraft. This clearly indicates that the troops or individuals who would be visiting Canada would be here with the consent of Canada, and that some provision has been made for them to be here lawfully.
The minister has explained what he considers to be the lawful requirements, so far as issuing the invitation for the troops to be present is concerned. I understand that this bill is really to implement the policy announced by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) on February 12 when he informed the house that steps had been taken, as a result of discussions by the joint board of defence, to ensure closer collaboration between the forces of Canada and the forces of the United, States. In, that statement the Prime Minister also emphasized the fact that- this in no way imperilled the relationship which exists and the close collaboration which was to continue between Canadian forces and the forces of the rest of the British commonwealth of nations.
In fact I believe it is a joint plan of Canada, the United States and Great Britain that this collaboration and cooperation, this joint study of defence problems should proceed and that there should be unification as far as possible of the weapons and equipment of the three countries. The Prime Minister stated that both governments, that is the Canadian and United States governments, believed that the decision which had been reached, namely to continue close collaboration, was a contribution to the stability of the world and to the establishment, through the united nations, of an effective system for world-wide security.
Visiting Forces

There are in this land today many people who believe that one way of ensuring world stability in the future, one way of avoiding a third world war, is for the peace-loving nations to have a reasonable degree of unity and a reasonable strength. We have had the bitter experience of the late thirties with its policy of appeasement, a policy under which we hardly dared to say "no" if somebody else shouted loudly "yes"; we had the bitter experience of that policy, and therefore I think a policy of ensuring that we have maximum cooperation and strength in order to maintain a peaceful world by cooperating with other nations which we know to be friendly is a sound and practical course to take.
We come now to the question of what type of individual or troops is to be permitted to come into Canada in accordance with the announcement made by the Prime Minister. He emphasized the fact, as reported on page 346 of Hansard of February 12, that they could come to the extent authorized by law. It may be that a request of the government is sufficient or that an invitation of the government may perhaps be considered as being authorized by law. Perhaps the minister will go into that in greater detail when we get into committee on the bill. The Prime Minister went on to say:
The collaboration will necessarily be limited and will be based on the following principles:
(1) Interchange of selected individuals so as to increase the familiarity of each country's defence establishment with that of the other country.
That would probably mean a few staff officers and instructors.
General cooperation and exchange of observers in connection with exercises . . .
No doubt there will be certain manoeuvres, exercises and experiments earned out not dissimilar to the Musk-Ox expedition of a few months ago. I can picture United State? observers and perhaps the observers of other countries coming here to gain from the experience of such exercises. Then the Prime Minister went on:
Encouragement of common designs and standards in arms, equipment, organization, methods of training and new developments.
There again one may readily understand the necessity, if we are to have a uniform system of equipment, of the Americans testing out those new weapons and that new equipment over our terrain and under our climatic conditions. We do not want to think only in terms of ground armament; there is the armament of the air as well. I am quite certain that it will be necessary for new equipment to be tested in our northern clime, but there

again only a few men would be required to carry out those experiments. Then the Prime Minister went on:
Mutual and reciprocal availability of military, naval and air facilities in each country.
That would be placing, shall we say, stations in the north at the disposal of the United States, so that they may come up and study conditions and, if necessary, operate from there. In those principles as laid down there, no mention was made of units. I suggest that the first time the possibility of units of the United States forces visiting this country was mentioned was when the minister referred to visits of United States units. That is putting a different complexion on the matter; that is going one step farther than the principles enunciated by the Prime Minister on February 12.
Mr. ST. LAURENT: If by using the word "unit" I conveyed to hon. members to whom technical military language may have special significance, something different from what was in the Prime Minister's statement, then I must apologize. The word was not used with the intention of signifying anything other than what was contained in the statement made by the Prime Minister on February 12. It may be my fault in using an expression which has a technical military significance which I did not attach to it.

I understand the term to mean a unit under the command of an officer. The definition of "unit" is given in the military textbooks, and I would certainly put that interpretation on the word. A battalion is a unit; a battery of artillery is a unit, and a regiment of tanks is a unit.
